chunks: What resistance is. The question: What is resistance?
Resistance is how strongly a material opposes the flow of current. We measure it as the voltage across a part divided by the current through it, R equals V over I , in ohms.
One ohm means one volt for each amp. The opposition comes from the electrons bumping into atoms, which also turns some of their energy into heat.
Picture people walking down a corridor. A longer corridor means more chances to bump into things, so it is harder going.
A wider corridor lets more people through, so it is easier. Rough, crowded flooring makes it harder still.
Resistance behaves the same way: it grows with length, shrinks as the conductor gets thicker (a bigger cross-section area), and depends on the material.
The analogy only captures the idea; real electrons are not individual walkers.
The resistor's I–V is a straight line, so V/I equals dV/dI everywhere.
The diode curve is nonlinear: V/I (the line from the origin to the point) is very different from the slope dV/dI = V T/I, which sets its small-signal resistance.
Ohm (Ω): the unit of resistance. One volt per amp. Resistivity ( ): how strongly a material resists current, regardless of its shape.
Conductor / insulator: a material with low resistivity, like copper, or very high resistivity, like glass. Joule heating: the heat produced when current flows through resistance.
Put 2 volts across a part and measure 4 milliamps. Then R equals 2 over 0. 004 equals 500 ohms. For shape, imagine a 1 m wire with 10 ohms.
A 2 m piece of the same wire is 20 ohms, because it is twice as long. A 2 m piece with twice the cross-section area is back to 10 ohms. That is the whole idea.
"Resistance is the opposition to current: R equals V over I, measured in ohms.
Physically, electrons drift through a material and keep scattering off the lattice and impurities, which limits the current for a given voltage and turns energy into heat.
For a uniform wire it's rho times length over area. V over I is a definition; Ohm's law says it's constant for ohmic materials like metals, but not for devices like diodes."
